newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kinkel proposes permanent "16+1" NATO committee.
newsitem.headline: Kinkel proposes permanent "16+1" NATO committee.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said on Sunday NATO should offer Russia a seat on a permanent consultation body for European security and said Germany would insist Russia's interests be considered by NATO.

Talking to the Welt am Sonntag newspaper, Kinkel said Russia should have equal rights with NATO members in the institution which he referred to as the "17 committee". It would be made up of the 16 NATO members plus Russia.
"The '16 plus one' should become a 'seventeen' security consultation committee, or in short S-17, in which NATO and Russia sit at one table with the same rights," said Kinkel.
He said the committee would have formal consultations on issues such as disarmament, non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, peace-keeping issues and other issues that interest both sides.
Foreign Ministers of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation will meet in Brussels later this week and review internal reforms necessary if the alliance's plans to expand eastwards are to go ahead.
The 16 ministers will also hold another session with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov whose country remains resolutely opposed to NATO's enlargement plans.
"Security will only happen in Europe with Russia, not by going past Russia or working without Russia," Kinkel said.
At his last meeting with Primakov, Kinkel assured him that Europe's security structure was not directed against anyone.
"Mistrust and worries about NATO expansion have not been overcome in Russia," he told the newspaper.
Western leaders have made clear time and again that the accession talks of at least some former communist states in eastern and central Europe will start next year whatever Moscow's objections.
However Russia wants to guarantee its interests in the post-expansion period.

NATO wants to formalise the relationship between the two former Cold War foes and the idea of a charter, covering all aspects of relations, has been around a long time. But little progress has been made on giving it substance.
British officials said on Friday NATO was considering whether to offer Russia a unique, three-tier security deal that could give Moscow a say in the running of the western alliance.
NATO wants to conclude the charter before a summit next year formally invites a handful of European countries to start negotiating membership.
Welt am Sonntag said diplomats had been working with Moscow on the charter for several months and Kinkel said Germany would insist on Russian security interests being considered.
Under the proposed plan, which British defence sources said was being heavily promoted by Germany, bilateral relations would be divided into three tiers:
- *one where NATO took decisions and told Moscow before they were implemented
- *one where NATO and Moscow held consultations on matters of joint interest
- one where NATO and Russia took joint decisions, which could effectively give Moscow the right of veto.

Defence sources said the crucial matter still to be decided was what matters the third tier would deal with, since Russia could be offended if it felt it was only being given the right to decide minor questions.
